notes.definition: Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction that happens continuously in living cells to supply the energy needed for living processes. It can be aerobic (using oxygen) or anaerobic (without oxygen).
explanation: Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens all the time in every living cell, in plants, animals and microorganisms. It is exothermic: it transfers energy from glucose to the surroundings and to the cell for living processes. Respiration is NOT the same as breathing. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is a reaction inside cells.

Organisms need the energy transferred by respiration for three main things: chemical reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones (for example making proteins from amino acids), movement (for example muscle contraction), and keeping warm (in mammals and birds, which keep a constant body temperature).

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and mostly takes place in the mitochondria. The word equation is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. With symbols: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose, so it transfers a lot of energy from each glucose molecule.

Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen. In muscle cells it produces lactic acid: glucose → lactic acid. In plant cells and yeast cells it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration in yeast is called fermentation. Anaerobic respiration transfers much less energy than aerobic respiration because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete: lactic acid and ethanol still contain a lot of energy.

Fermentation by yeast is economically important. In bread-making, the carbon dioxide produced makes the dough rise, and the ethanol evaporates during baking. In brewing beer and making wine, the ethanol is the alcohol in the drink. Carbon dioxide can be detected with limewater, which turns milky (cloudy) when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
keyFacts: Respiration is exothermic and happens continuously in all living cells.
Energy from respiration is used to build larger molecules, for movement and for keeping warm.
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Symbols: C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose), O₂ (oxygen), CO₂ (carbon dioxide), H₂O (water).
Anaerobic in muscles: glucose → lactic acid.
Anaerobic in plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (fermentation in yeast).
Anaerobic respiration transfers much less energy because glucose is only partly (incompletely) oxidised.
Aerobic respiration happens mainly in the mitochondria.
Yeast fermentation is used to make bread (carbon dioxide) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol).
Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.

keyTerms.definition: An exothermic reaction in living cells that transfers energy from glucose for living processes.
Respiration using oxygen: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Respiration without oxygen; produces lactic acid in muscles, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in plants and yeast.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings.
The product of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the right equation
workedExamples.question: Write the word equation for respiration in (a) a running muscle with plenty of oxygen, (b) a sprinting muscle short of oxygen, (c) yeast in a sealed container.
steps: (a) Oxygen is available, so it is aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
(b) No oxygen in a muscle cell, so anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid.
(c) No oxygen in yeast, so fermentation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
workedExamples.answer: (a) glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; (b) glucose → lactic acid; (c) glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide

workedExamples.title: Calculating a rate of fermentation
workedExamples.question: Yeast in glucose solution produced 21 cm³ of carbon dioxide in 7 minutes. Calculate the rate of carbon dioxide production.

workedExamples.title: Comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration
workedExamples.question: Give three differences between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells.
steps: Oxygen: aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not.
Products: aerobic makes carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic makes lactic acid.
Energy: aerobic transfers much more energy per glucose; anaerobic transfers less because glucose is incompletely oxidised.
workedExamples.answer: Oxygen needed or not; different products; aerobic transfers much more energy.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think respiration is the same as breathing.
misconceptions.right: In fact respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that transfers energy. Breathing (ventilation) just moves air in and out of the lungs.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think respiration 'makes' or 'produces' energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact energy cannot be made. Respiration transfers energy that was stored in glucose.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think anaerobic respiration in muscles produces carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact anaerobic respiration in muscle cells produces only lactic acid. It is anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells that produces carbon dioxide (with ethanol).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants only photosynthesise and do not respire.
misconceptions.right: In fact plant cells respire all the time, day and night, just like animal cells.

realWorld: Bakers add yeast to bread dough; the carbon dioxide from fermentation makes the dough rise, and the ethanol evaporates in the oven.
Brewers and winemakers use yeast fermentation to produce the ethanol in beer and wine.
Plant roots in waterlogged soil can run short of oxygen and respire anaerobically, producing ethanol, which can damage the roots.
Sprinters rely partly on anaerobic respiration in their muscles during a 100 m race, which is why lactic acid builds up.
examTips: Always say respiration 'transfers' or 'releases' energy, never 'makes' or 'produces' energy.
Check which organism the question is about: lactic acid for animal muscles, ethanol and carbon dioxide for plants and yeast.
To explain why anaerobic respiration transfers less energy, use the phrase 'incomplete oxidation of glucose'.
In comparison questions, make each point a direct comparison, for example 'aerobic uses oxygen but anaerobic does not'.
summary: Respiration is an exothermic reaction happening continuously in all living cells.
Energy is used for building larger molecules, movement and keeping warm.
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Anaerobic in muscles: glucose → lactic acid.
Anaerobic in plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (fermentation).
Anaerobic transfers much less energy because glucose is incompletely oxidised.
Fermentation is used to make bread and alcoholic drinks.

questions.question: Which substance is needed for aerobic respiration?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: 'Aerobic' means 'with oxygen'. Carbon dioxide is a product, not a reactant. Lactic acid and ethanol are products of anaerobic respiration.

questions.question: What are the products of aerobic respiration?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants. Lactic acid, and ethanol with carbon dioxide, are products of anaerobic respiration.

questions.question: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?
markScheme: 1 mark: lactic acid
questions.explanation: In muscle cells, glucose → lactic acid. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are made by anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells. Carbon dioxide and water come from aerobic respiration.

questions.question: What does yeast produce when it respires anaerobically?
markScheme: 1 mark: ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Fermentation in yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is made in animal muscle cells. Glucose is the reactant, not the product.

questions.question: Why does anaerobic respiration transfer much less energy than aerobic respiration?
options: The oxidation of glucose is incomplete
It only happens in muscle cells
markScheme: 1 mark: the oxidation of glucose is incomplete
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, glucose is only partly broken down. Much of the energy stays in lactic acid or ethanol. Anaerobic respiration also happens in yeast and plants, so it is not limited to muscles.

questions.question: Respiration is an exothermic reaction. What does this mean?
options: It takes in energy from the surroundings
It transfers energy to the surroundings
It only happens when an organism is moving
markScheme: 1 mark: it transfers energy to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, which is why respiring cells warm up. Taking in energy describes an endothermic reaction such as photosynthesis.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows an animal cell.
In which part of the cell does most aerobic respiration take place?

markScheme: 1 mark: A (mitochondria)
questions.explanation: A is a mitochondrion, the site of aerobic respiration. B is the nucleus, which controls the cell; C is the cell membrane and D is the cytoplasm, where anaerobic respiration happens but not most aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Animals use energy from respiration for several purposes. Which of these is NOT one of them?
options: Building larger molecules from smaller ones
Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water
markScheme: 1 mark: making glucose from carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water is photosynthesis, which uses energy from light and does not happen in animals. The other three are the main uses of energy from respiration.

questions.question: Why is yeast added to bread dough?
options: Its ethanol makes the bread taste sweet
Its carbon dioxide makes the dough rise
Its lactic acid makes the bread sour
Its oxygen makes the bread light
markScheme: 1 mark: its carbon dioxide makes the dough rise
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugars in the dough and produces carbon dioxide bubbles, which make the dough rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking. Yeast does not produce lactic acid or oxygen.

questions.question: Which pair shows the chemical formulae of the two reactants in aerobic respiration?
markScheme: 1 mark: C₆H₁₂O₆ and O₂
questions.explanation: The reactants are glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) and oxygen (O₂). CO₂ and H₂O are the products of aerobic respiration (and the reactants of photosynthesis).

questions.question: The soil around a plant becomes waterlogged, so its root cells are short of oxygen. Which substances will the root cells produce by anaerobic respiration?
markScheme: 1 mark: ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Plant cells respire anaerobically in the same way as yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is the product in animal muscle cells. Carbon dioxide and water come from aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.

questions.question: When does respiration take place?
options: Only at night in plant cells
markScheme: 1 mark: continuously in all living cells
questions.explanation: All living cells need a constant supply of energy, so respiration never stops. Plants respire day and night, not only when it is dark.

questions.question: Which statement comparing types of respiration is correct?
options: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces ethanol
Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces carbon dioxide, but anaerobic respiration in muscles does not
Anaerobic respiration transfers more energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration
Both aerobic and anaerobic respiration always produce water
markScheme: 1 mark: anaerobic respiration in yeast produces carbon dioxide, but anaerobic respiration in muscles does not
questions.explanation: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles make only lactic acid. Anaerobic respiration transfers much less energy, and water is only a product of aerobic respiration.

questions.question:
Complete the word equation for aerobic respiration.
........ + ........ → ........ + ........
markScheme: 1 mark: reactants glucose + oxygen
1 mark: products carbon dioxide + water
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration is the reverse of the overall photosynthesis equation. Do not write 'energy' as a product: energy is transferred, but it is not a substance.

questions.question:
Complete the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscle cells.
glucose → ........
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose → lactic acid
questions.explanation: There is only one reactant (glucose) and one product (lactic acid). No oxygen is used and no carbon dioxide is produced.

questions.question: Give two ways in which animals use the energy transferred by respiration.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: chemical reactions to build larger molecules; movement / muscle contraction; keeping warm
questions.explanation: The specification lists three uses: building larger molecules, movement and keeping warm. Vague answers like 'to live' do not get marks.

questions.question:
Complete the word equation for anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in yeast cells.
glucose → ........ + ........
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose → ethanol
1 mark: + carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast. Remember that no oxygen is a reactant and no water is produced.

questions.question: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in muscle cells. Give three differences.
markScheme: 1 mark: aerobic needs oxygen but anaerobic does not
1 mark: aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water but anaerobic produces lactic acid
1 mark: aerobic transfers much more energy per glucose than anaerobic (incomplete oxidation)
questions.explanation: Each comparison should mention both types. A similarity (both use glucose) does not count as a difference.

questions.question: Explain why yeast is important in making bread and in brewing beer.
markScheme: 1 mark: in bread-making, carbon dioxide from fermentation makes the dough rise
1 mark: in brewing, fermentation produces ethanol (alcohol)
questions.explanation: The same reaction, glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, is useful in two ways: bakers want the gas, brewers want the alcohol.

questions.question:
A student investigated respiration in yeast.
Figure 1 shows the apparatus.
After 20 minutes the limewater turned milky.
Explain the purpose of the layer of oil and what the result shows.

markScheme: 1 mark: the oil stops oxygen from the air entering the solution
1 mark: so the yeast respires anaerobically (fermentation)
1 mark: limewater turning milky shows carbon dioxide was produced
questions.explanation: The layer of oil creates anaerobic conditions. Yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

questions.question: Explain why anaerobic respiration transfers less energy from each glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
markScheme: 1 mark: the oxidation of glucose is incomplete / glucose is not fully broken down
1 mark: so energy remains stored in the product (lactic acid or ethanol)
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose all the way down to carbon dioxide and water. In anaerobic respiration much of the energy remains locked up in lactic acid or ethanol.

questions.question: Describe the test for carbon dioxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: bubble the gas through limewater, which turns milky / cloudy
questions.explanation: Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide. A glowing splint is the test for oxygen, and a lighted splint is the test for hydrogen.

markScheme: 1 mark: volume at 6 minutes read as 18 cm³ and 18 ÷ 6
1 mark: 3 cm³/min
questions.explanation: From Figure 1, the volume at 6 minutes is 18 cm³. Mean rate = volume ÷ time = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 cm³ per minute.

questions.question:
A student measured the volume of carbon dioxide produced by yeast in 10 minutes at two temperatures.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage increase in the volume of carbon dioxide produced when the temperature was raised from 20 °C to 30 °C.

headers: Volume of carbon dioxide produced in 10 minutes in cm³

markScheme: 1 mark: 150%
questions.explanation: Increase = 30 − 12 = 18 cm³. Percentage increase = 18 ÷ 12 × 100 = 150%. Dividing by 30 instead of the original value gives 60%, which is wrong.

questions.question:
A student measured the rate of carbon dioxide production by yeast three times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean rate of carbon dioxide production.

headers: Rate of carbon dioxide production in cm³/min

questions.explanation: Add the values (7.8) and divide by the number of values (3) to get 2.6 cm³/min.

questions.question:
A student measured the volume of a piece of bread dough containing yeast as it was left in a warm place.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean rate of increase in volume of the dough over the 40 minutes.
Give your answer in cm³ per minute.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.75 cm³/min
questions.explanation: Change in volume = 120 − 50 = 70 cm³. Rate = 70 ÷ 40 = 1.75 cm³/min. Using 120 ÷ 40 = 3 forgets to subtract the starting volume.

questions.question:
At 20 °C, yeast produced carbon dioxide at a rate of 1.2 cm³/min.
At 35 °C the rate was 2.5 times faster.
Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced by the yeast at 35 °C in 15 minutes.
markScheme: 1 mark: rate at 35 °C = 1.2 × 2.5 = 3.0 cm³/min
1 mark: volume = 3.0 × 15 = 45 cm³
questions.explanation: First find the new rate (3.0 cm³/min), then multiply by the time. Volume = rate × time = 3.0 × 15 = 45 cm³.

questions.question: Describe how anaerobic respiration in yeast is used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.
markScheme: Indicative content: anaerobic respiration in yeast is called fermentation; glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide; in bread-making, yeast is mixed into dough with sugar and kept warm; carbon dioxide bubbles make the dough rise; ethanol evaporates during baking; in brewing / winemaking, yeast ferments sugars (from grain or grapes) without oxygen; the ethanol produced is the alcohol in the drink; carbon dioxide can give fizz.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of fermentation, including the products, linked correctly to both bread and alcoholic drinks.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct points, for example naming a product or one use, with little linking.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Both industries use the same reaction. The key is to match each product to its use: carbon dioxide for bread, ethanol for drinks.

questions.question: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in animal muscle cells and in yeast cells.
markScheme: Indicative content: all three use glucose and are exothermic, transferring energy; aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not; aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; anaerobic in muscles: glucose → lactic acid; anaerobic in yeast (fermentation): glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide; both aerobic and yeast fermentation produce carbon dioxide, but muscle anaerobic respiration does not; aerobic transfers much more energy per glucose; anaerobic transfers much less because oxidation of glucose is incomplete; aerobic takes place mainly in mitochondria; anaerobic respiration happens when oxygen is in short supply (e.g. vigorous exercise, sealed fermentation vessel); yeast fermentation is used for bread and alcoholic drinks.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed comparison covering oxygen use, products of all three types and energy transferred, with an explanation (incomplete oxidation) and both similarities and differences.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): compares at least two types correctly, including products and oxygen use, with some reference to energy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two types with little comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A top-level answer uses comparative language (both, whereas, but) and covers reactants, products, oxygen, energy and the reason for the energy difference, for all three types.
